summary: At 24 people per square mile spread across 2,273 square miles, Tuolumne County is roughly the size of Delaware yet holds fewer residents than a mid-sized college campus — and a significant chunk of that acreage is Yosemite National Park's western gateway, with Highways 108 and 120 serving as literal on-ramps to some of the most dramatic granite scenery on Earth. The county seat of Sonora anchors a small historic Gold Rush-era downtown along Highway 49, where the economy leans heavily on healthcare (Adventist Health Sonora is one of the largest employers), tourism, public-sector jobs, and timber — which means switching employers without a long drive is genuinely constrained. A median home price of $406,200 against a median household income of $72,259 produces a price-to-income ratio around 5.6, more affordable than much of coastal California but still a stretch on a single local salary, especially since rents averaging $1,247 suggest limited rental stock. Daily highs average only 60°F annually, with 9.2 hours of sunshine per day — winter nights dip well below freezing at elevation, and summer days in the lower foothills can spike hot, making the climate a study in contrasts depending on exactly where you land between 1,000 and 8,000 feet. The terrain is canyon-carved Sierra Nevada foothill country: ponderosa pines, seasonal wildflower meadows, and views of snowcapped ridgelines — gorgeous, but the hilly topography and sparse density mean errands involve driving, not walking. Tuolumne offers extraordinary proximity to wilderness at a housing cost that would buy a modest condo in the Bay Area, but the tradeoff is a thin job market and the kind of isolation that either liberates or confines, depending on how often you need to be somewhere else.
